newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. envoy in bid to seal Israel-PLO Hebron deal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy in bid to seal Israel-PLO Hebron deal.

text.p: U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross tried to seal an Israeli-PLO deal on the West Bank town of Hebron on Sunday, saying a coming trip by Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to Europe would hamper mediation efforts.

Ross met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday and Israel Radio said he would travel to the Gaza Strip for talks with Arafat. The envoy said Israelis and Palestinians still had differences to overcome.
Earlier on Sunday, Jewish settlers said Netanyahu's government had put up for sale 3,000 apartments completed years ago in West Bank settlements.
"It's clear that we have further narrowed the differences that exist but we have not overcome those differences," Ross told reporters after meeting Netanyahu in northern Israel.

"Clearly the pace of negotiations is affected when the leaders are not here. Also my own presence is affected when the leaders aren't here because part of my mission is very clearly to go back and forth between the leaders," Ross said.
Arafat was due to leave Gaza on Monday on a European tour of several days.
An Israeli official had said the two sides were on the verge of an agreement which could be concluded at an Israeli-Palestinian summit on Sunday. But Palestinians said they were still far apart.

Netanyahu's top adviser David Bar-Illan said Israeli and Palestinian negotiators had agreed on most details for implementing the long-overdue Israeli redeployment in Hebron and were awaiting Arafat's consent.
Asked if Netanyahu would meet Arafat on Sunday, Bar-Illan said: "It may happen."
But Arafat's aide Nabil Abu Rdainah said no arrangements had been made for a summit with Netanyahu.
"There are deep differences between the two positions. The same disputed issues are still disputed," said Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat.
He said the differences included Israel's demand for the right to pursue Palestinian militants into parts of Hebron vacated by Israel and what weapons Palestinian police would carry.

Israel's former Labour government agreed more than a year ago to redeploy troops away from Hebron, home to 100,000 Palestinians and 400 Jewish settlers, but delayed the pullout after suicide bombings by Moslem militants killed 59 people in the Jewish state in February and March.

The right-wing Netanyahu, who swept to power in elections last May capitalising on Israeli security fears heightened by the bombings, has insisted on adjusting the agreement to help safeguard Jewish settlers in the West Ban town.
Netanyahu's handling of peace talks and his settlement policy in the West Bank and Gaza Strip where 130,000 Jews live among two million Palestinians have angered his Arab peace partners.

Netanyahu lifted the previous government's restrictions on settlement activity in August. Settlers said on Sunday technical details which had held up sale of the 3,000 empty apartments in the West Bank settlements had now been overcome.
"Prices were set for the apartments and the marketing has begun," said settler leader Aharon Domb. A government spokesman said he was checking the report.
The apartments were completed years ago but Israel's Labour government had blocked their sale.
